key: Why such an odd number? It was chosen
alt: Eight samples, each on a round white paper on a black background, arranged in two rows and labeled with their masses. Top row: 65.4 g Zn, a small pile of gray powder; 12.0 g C, black lumps; 24.3 g Mg, a pile of gray metal turnings; 63.5 g Cu, a coil of copper wire. Bottom row: 32.1 g S, pale yellow powder; 28.1 g Si, a few shiny gray-blue chunks; 207 g Pb, a pile of dark gray granules; 118.7 g Sn, silvery lumps of tin.
caption: One mole each of eight elements. Every sample holds the same number of atoms, 6.0221 × 10<sup>23</sup>, but the masses differ, because each mass in grams matches the element’s atomic mass on the periodic table.
credit_extra: photo: modification of work by Mark Ott
why: Real photo of the "same count, different mass" idea; 5.1 explains it only in words (5.2 has a 4-sample diagram, not photos of elements).

key: s number dwarfs even the biggest counts in biology
lead: Biology also runs on counts far smaller than a mole. When one nerve cell signals the next, it releases neurotransmitter molecules, such as dopamine, C8H11NO2, from tiny sacs called vesicles into the narrow gap between the cells, the synapse. Neuroscientists who measure these releases count molecules, and Avogadro’s number turns those counts into moles: even one million dopamine molecules is only 1.7 × 10−18 mol.
alt: Two drawings. (a) A small sketch of a nerve cell with a long branching fiber; an arrow leads to an enlarged view of the fiber’s rounded end, labeled Neuron, which holds many round vesicles filled with small green dots. Some vesicles have opened at the bottom edge and released the dots, labeled Neurotransmitters, into a narrow gap labeled Synapse, just above the surface of a second cell, also labeled Neuron. (b) A ball-and-stick model of dopamine: a ring of six black carbon atoms with white hydrogens; two neighboring ring carbons each carry a red oxygen with a white hydrogen, and a chain of two black carbons leads from the ring to a blue nitrogen with two white hydrogens.
caption: (a) Nerve cells signal by releasing neurotransmitter molecules from vesicles into the synapse between cells. (b) A model of dopamine, C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>11</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>, a neurotransmitter involved in movement and reward. Counts of molecules this small are converted to moles with Avogadro’s number.
why: Biology tie (OpenStax "Counting Neurotransmitter Molecules" feature) for the mole as a count; adds the small-count side to the existing Biology Connection.

key: Set up molar mass problems as a small table
alt: A table with columns Element, Quantity, times sign, Average atomic mass (amu), equals sign, and Subtotal. Row Na: 1 times 22.99 equals 22.99. Row Cl: 1 times 35.45 equals 35.45. Bottom row: Formula mass, 58.44. Beside the table, a model of a small cube of sodium chloride: purple and green spheres alternate at the corners of eight stacked cubes, joined by sticks.
caption: The small table from the Professor Tip, filled in for sodium chloride: element, number of atoms, atomic mass, and subtotal. The formula mass of NaCl is 58.44 amu, so its molar mass is 58.44 g/mol, the same masses as on the yellow sheet.
why: Shows the exact setup the Professor Tip describes (element, count, mass, subtotal); NaCl values match the yellow sheet. (The OpenStax aspirin/chloroform tables use 12.01 and 16.00, not yellow-sheet masses, so they were skipped.)

key: there is a ratio hidden in plain sight
alt: Four labeled drawings made of white spheres. H: one sphere, labeled One H atom. 2H: two separate spheres, labeled Two H atoms. H2 (subscript 2): two spheres joined together, labeled One H2 molecule. 2H2: two pairs of joined spheres, labeled Two H2 molecules.
caption: A coefficient and a subscript do not mean the same thing. H is one atom and 2H is two separate atoms, but H<sub>2</sub> is one molecule made of two atoms, and 2H<sub>2</sub> is two molecules holding four atoms. One mole of H<sub>2</sub> therefore contains two moles of H atoms.
why: Picture for the diatomic trap: atoms vs. diatomic molecules, coefficient vs. subscript.

lead: The ionic compound looks nothing like the elements that formed it. Sodium is a soft, shiny metal so reactive that it is stored under oil, and chlorine is a poisonous yellow-green gas, yet together they form ordinary table salt.
alt: Three photographs. (a) A glass vial of clear oil holding a curled, soft, silvery-gray piece of sodium metal. (b) A capped glass bottle filled with pale yellow-green gas: chlorine. (c) A spoon heaped with white crystals of table salt.
caption: (a) Sodium, a soft metal stored under mineral oil to keep it from reacting with air and water. (b) Chlorine, a pale yellow-green gas. (c) Sodium chloride, the white crystalline ionic compound they form.
credit_extra: photo a: modification of work by “Jurii”/Wikimedia Commons
why: Real photos of Na, Cl2 and NaCl: shows that an ionic compound has entirely new properties; 6.1 has only a diagram.

key: huge, repeating three-dimensional array of ions called a
alt: Two models of a sodium chloride crystal. (a) A space-filling cube of touching spheres, larger green spheres alternating with smaller purple ones in every direction. (b) An expanded view of the same arrangement with the spheres pulled apart and joined by gray sticks, one green sphere labeled Cl minus and one purple sphere labeled Na plus; each sphere is surrounded by spheres of the other color.
caption: The crystal lattice of sodium chloride. (a) Na<sup>+</sup> ions (purple) and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions (green) packed together. (b) An expanded view: each ion is surrounded by six ions of the opposite charge, and no single NaCl “molecule” can be picked out.
why: Visual of the crystal lattice and formula units (no molecules) that 6.1 describes only in words.

key: Lone pairs spread out a little more than bonding pairs
alt: Three views of ammonia. (a) Four orange electron-cloud lobes point to the corners of a tetrahedron drawn with dashed green lines; the top lobe holds two dots and is labeled Lone pair. (b) A ball-and-stick model with a blue nitrogen atom on top and three white hydrogen atoms below it, forming a pyramid over a dashed triangular base. (c) The same lobes as in (a), with curved arrows showing the lone pair pushing the three bonding lobes closer together; the angle between two bonds is labeled 106.8 degrees.
caption: Ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>: 4 groups, 1 lone pair. (a) The electron-group geometry is tetrahedral. (b) The shape, which names only the atoms, is trigonal pyramidal. (c) The lone pair pushes the bonds closer together, so the H–N–H angle is about 107°, a little less than 109.5°.
why: Shows electron-group geometry vs. molecular shape and lone-pair squeeze (107 degrees) in one figure; vsepr_shapes.svg shows the six shapes but not this distinction or the real angle.

key: A covalent bond is like two friends splitting an order of fries
alt: Two drawings of hydrogen chloride. (a) A small white sphere for H overlaps a larger green sphere for Cl, with a dot at each nucleus; a green haze of electron density is thicker around the chlorine end. Above them, a dipole arrow with a cross at the H end points toward Cl. (b) The structural formula H–Cl with delta plus above H and delta minus above Cl.
caption: A polar bond. (a) In HCl the shared electrons spend more time near chlorine, the more electronegative atom, so the electron cloud is lopsided; the dipole arrow points toward Cl. (b) The same bond with partial charges, δ+ on H and δ− on Cl. With yellow-sheet values, ΔEN = 3.0 − 2.1 = 0.9: polar covalent.
why: Picture of the "uneven electron cloud" plus the dipole-arrow and delta notation the section teaches; polarity.svg shows molecules, not the electron cloud of one bond.
